pr.title: coverage: Count await when the Future is immediately ready
pr.description:
Currently `await` is only counted towards coverage if the containing
function is suspended and resumed at least once. This is because it
expands to code which contains a branch on the discriminant of `Poll`.

By treating it like a branching macro (e.g. `assert!`), these
implementation details will be hidden from the coverage results.

I added a test to ensure the fix works in simple cases, but the heuristic of picking only the first await-related covspan might be unreliable. I plan on testing more thoroughly with a real codebase over the next couple of weeks.

closes #98712
pr.author: jonathan-conder

analysis.originalLogic: Coverage span extraction recorded only an optional visible bang-macro name (`visible_macro: Option<Symbol>`) for macro-expanded spans. The span-refinement pass sorted covspans in dominator order, then called `remove_unwanted_macro_spans`, which dropped duplicate macro-expanded covspans but explicitly retained all non-macro spans. `split_visible_macro_spans` likewise split only spans with a visible macro name. Consequently, spans arising from `await` desugaring were treated as ordinary non-macro spans and were not deduplicated/hidden.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect behavior was to let `await`-desugared coverage spans remain as ordinary spans rather than treating the await expansion like a branching macro. Because `await` expands into a branch on the `Poll` discriminant, coverage mappings exposed implementation-detail regions that are only reached when the future is polled again after suspension. As the PR says, currently `await` is only counted towards coverage if the containing function is suspended and resumed at least once. This is the wrong transformation to compare against: same instrumented async function, but await-related expansion spans are retained instead of deduplicating them by span in dominator order.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust source compiled with MIR coverage instrumentation (`instrument-coverage`) that contains an `.await` in an async function. The key case is a future that is immediately ready and never suspends (for example, an async fn returning a value, polled through a noop waker executor). It also includes async functions with conditional/match arms containing awaits, where await-related spans can appear in multiple coverage blocks.
analysis.summary: InstrumentCoverage previously recognized only bang macro expansions when deduplicating/unexpanding coverage spans, so `await` desugaring exposed its `Poll` discriminant branch and await coverage depended on the future actually suspending and resuming. The fix generalizes `visible_macro: Option<Symbol>` to `expn_kind: Option<ExpnKind>` and deduplicates both `DesugaringKind::Await` and bang-macro spans by span, keeping the first in dominator order, while continuing to split only visible bang macros.
analysis.trigger: An async function under coverage instrumentation contains an `.await` whose future completes without ever yielding; without special handling of the await desugaring, the await's coverage is not counted as expected. Conditional match expressions with multiple awaits also produce duplicate await-related span mappings that need collapsing.
preconditions: Coverage instrumentation is enabled for the async function containing the await.
Covspans have been sorted in BCB dominator order before deduplication, so the retained first span is likely to dominate the others.
The await future may be immediately ready and never suspend/resume the enclosing async function.
pitfalls: Do not treat every expansion kind like a visible bang macro: `split_visible_macro_spans` must only split `ExpnKind::Macro(MacroKind::Bang, visible_macro)` spans. Await desugaring has no visible macro name to split.
Do not deduplicate all spans indiscriminately; retain non-await, non-bang-macro spans unchanged.
Keep the first await-related or bang-macro covspan per identical span in dominator order, not an arbitrary one; the source notes the retained first span is likely to dominate the others.
The PR itself warns that the heuristic of picking only the first await-related covspan might be unreliable, so tests should cover more than the simple ready-future case.
Do not conflate hiding await's internal Poll-discriminant branch with changing the async lowering itself; the fix is in coverage span refinement, not in await code generation.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a coverage test with a noop-waker executor and an async function that awaits an immediately ready future; assert that the await/line coverage is reported even though the async function never suspends. Use the patch's `tests/coverage/await_ready.rs` shape: `#[coverage(off)] async fn ready() -> u8 { 1 }`, `async fn await_ready() -> u8 { ready().await }`, and a `block_on` loop using `core::task::Waker::noop()`. Also inspect updated `tests/coverage/async.cov-map` expectations: await-related mappings collapse (e.g. file mappings drop from 13 to 11 and separate `(prev + 0, 14) to (start + 0, 17)` / `(prev + 0, 18) to ...` mappings merge into `(prev + 0, 14) to (start + 0, 23)`). For differential testing, compare an immediately-ready await against a future that yields at least once; under the old span treatment only the yielding case gets the await counted, while the corrected treatment should make await coverage independent of suspension.
